citations.desc: Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC).
citations.narrative:
For protocol 2023-0282, the principal investigator did not provide a written narrative description of the methods used to
determine that alternatives to painful procedures were not available.
The written narrative described literature searches focused on the study’s scientific aims; however, these searches did not
address alternatives to several procedures described in the protocol that may cause more than momentary or slight pain
or distress, including major abdominal surgery with multi catheter implantation, sepsis induction, intragastric tube
‑
insertion, enteral feeding, and repeated muscle biopsies. These procedures involve tissue manipulation or physiologic
stress, yet the protocol did not document searches for alternatives for these procedures.
When the investigator does not provide a written narrative that addresses alternatives to all painful or distressful
procedures, the IACUC cannot effectively review the proposal to determine that the principal investigator has considered
alternatives to these procedures. Additionally, the animals may experience unnecessary pain and distress if alternatives
are available but not considered.
The IACUC shall determine that the principal investigator has considered alternatives to procedures that may cause more
than momentary pain or distress to the animals and has provided a written narrative description of the methods and
sources used to determine that alternatives were not available.
Correct by: August 20, 2026

citations.desc: Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC).
citations.narrative:
Proposals to conduct an activity using animals do not contain a complete description of the proposed use of the animals.
An internal IACUC review notes that protocol 2023-0282 did not contain sufficient procedural detail for catheter anchoring,
gastric tube verification, postoperative monitoring, temperature requirements, or sepsis day monitoring intervals. As a
result, the IACUC could not determine how the procedures would be performed, how the animals would be monitored, or
whether the proposed activities met the regulatory requirements for ensuring the animals’ health, comfort, and appropriate
safeguards.
The combined teaching/research horse protocol (protocols 2024 0002 CA and 2024 0263 CA) did not clearly distinguish
the use of horses for non-regulated agricultural research and regulated teaching. As a result, the IACUC could not
determine what procedures horses would experience as part of which animal use activity or the number and type of
procedures an individual horse would experience. The IACUC’s internal review documented one euthanasia event
involving USDA covered horses following complications associated with reproductive procedures conducted under the
original combined teaching and research protocol. This lack of clarity made it difficult for the IACUC to determine which
animals would undergo specific procedures, the number and type of procedures an individual horse would experience,
and the conditions under which those procedures would occur. These reproductive procedures, including transvaginal
follicular aspiration (TVA) and rectal palpation/manipulation, require clear protocol descriptions because they involve
direct physical interaction, restraint, and postoperative monitoring. Without complete information describing how and when
these procedures would be performed, the IACUC was unable to evaluate whether the proposed activities met regulatory
requirements and whether appropriate safeguards and review processes were in place to ensure animal welfare. The
IACUC’s uncertainty resulted in reclassification of both protocols from Category C to Category D, reflecting that the
procedures described in the protocol involved more than slight pain or discomfort and required additional oversight.
When animal use protocols do not adequately describe the proposed use of the animals, the IACUC cannot effectively
review the procedures to verify compliance with the Animal Welfare Regulations or to ensure the welfare of the animals.
Proposals to conduct activities involving animals must contain a complete description of the proposed use of the animals.
Correct by: August 20, 2026

The facility did not handle animals as carefully as possible in a manner that does not cause trauma, physical harm, or
unnecessary discomfort.
Records associated with protocol 2023 0282 document that at least three animals required euthanasia as a result of not
properly verifying, securing, and/or monitoring animals with feeding tubes.
Necropsies for pigs CH, CE, and CG documented peritonitis from gastrointestinal leakage associated with gastric tube
displacement and “feeding into (the) peritoneal cavity”. The facility records noted that these events occurred after
retraining on proper procedures. The facility determined, via necropsy and their internal investigation, that this increased
rate of adverse events resulted from not following instructions regarding verification of gastric tube placement and
aspiration checks prior to feeding.
The IACUC’s internal review documented that the procedural room on the day of CI’s sepsis induction was cold and that
the ambient temperature was not known. Because handling of all animals shall be done as expeditiously and carefully as
possible in a manner that does not cause trauma, overheating, excessive cooling, behavioral stress, physical harm, or
unnecessary discomfort, unrecognized low environmental temperatures during a prolonged sepsis procedure reduce the
ability to prevent excessive cooling and to maintain the animal’s condition stability. Swine undergoing anesthesia and
sepsis induction are vulnerable to rapid shifts in thermal regulation, and maintaining appropriate temperature is an
important component of careful handling in these procedures. The protocol required use of a temperature transponder to
provide continuous core temperature trends and alarms during sepsis, allowing timely detection of temperature changes
that may indicate physiologic instability. However, staff used a rectal thermometer because the transponder device was
not functional due to failure to charge the battery. Intermittent rectal readings do not provide real time trend information
and can miss early temperature changes, reducing the ability to take timely, careful action to prevent behavioral stress or
physical harm. In this context, the combination of a cold procedural room, unknown ambient temperature, and lack of
continuous temperature monitoring demonstrates that handling did not occur in a manner that carefully protected the
animal from excessive cooling or physiologic instability during sepsis induction. These conditions, documented in the
internal review and associated records, show that the handling did not fully meet the regulatory requirement to ensure
animals are managed in a manner that does not cause excessive cooling, physical harm, or unnecessary discomfort.
Failure to follow training and instruction that has been provided via protocols, veterinarians, and other guidance
documents does not ensure that handling of animals is done as carefully as possible. Mishandling of animals can lead to
serious consequences such as animal illness, injury, pain, distress, or death. The facility must ensure that handling of all
animals shall be done as expeditiously and carefully as possible in a manner that does not cause trauma, excessive
cooling, behavioral stress, physical harm, and unnecessary discomfort.
Correct by: August 20, 2026
